title: Real World Development with GitHub Copilot and VS Code — Harald Kirschner, Christopher Harrison
talk_summary: A VS Code/Copilot team workshop walking through 'vibe coding' maturity stages (yolo, structured, spec-driven), demoing agent mode, custom instructions, reusable prompts, custom chat modes, tool sets, and MCP servers. The transferable mechanisms are scoped instruction files, reusable task prompts, tool restriction per mode, and spec-first planning — not the demo apps.

takeaways.technique: Scoped instruction files with glob front-matter
takeaways.what_they_do: Instructions live in repo files; a global one gives stack grounding, and per-glob files apply only to matching file types so rules stay small and non-conflicting instead of one monolith.
takeaways.evidence_quote: these become rather monolith and large and unwieldy ... they start to be scoped with a glob pattern

takeaways.technique: Reusable task prompts as versioned files
takeaways.what_they_do: A hand-tuned prompt that reliably one-shots a task (e.g. writing tests) is stored as a slash-invokable file in the repo so the whole team uses the same one instead of copy-pasting from Slack.
takeaways.evidence_quote: your AI champion in the team handcraft this this perfect prompt which oneshots your test consistently and now everybody shares it in Slack

takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of exposing every MCP tool to every request (tool explosion), they define named tool sets and bind a mode/prompt to only the tools it needs; they also warn that a mode referencing nonexistent tools silently degrades to plain chat.
Separate modes for writing the spec, writing the implementation plan, then implementing; feed meeting transcripts in and have the model argue/critique the spec before coding.
takeaways.evidence_quote: write the spec write the plan and then implement. So you would even have three modes if you do it correctly

takeaways.technique: Deterministic checks wired into the agent loop
takeaways.what_they_do: They stress that linting/tasks must be set up in the template so the agent can run tests and read problems/output itself; TDD mode writes failing tests, gets confirmation, then implements and re-runs tests.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if you have tasks set up and you have linting set up, things will just work. So make sure those are set up in your template

takeaways.what_they_do: Agent edits are checkpointed so you can revert to any prior stage, and the guidance is to commit at every working state so the agent can keep experimenting safely.
takeaways.evidence_quote: anytime you have a working state, just make sure you commit it so AI can continue making mistakes and be creative
